Election 2026: Has vote splitting saved a battered coalition?
Daily News

Politics

Election 2026: Has vote splitting saved a battered coalition?

NZ · Major · Catch up

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Analysis of the 2026 New Zealand election indicates that a vote-splitting campaign, where voters supported National candidates while giving party votes to ACT or NZ First, helped the National Party retain a stable number of electorate seats despite losing approximately 9 percentage points of party vote support. National candidates outperformed the party vote by a median of 17.2 points in seats they won, while ACT and NZ First gained roughly six percentage points combined.

Why it matters

The outcome leaves Prime Minister Christopher Luxon with the weakest negotiating position for coalition talks in history, as the National Party is severely diminished despite retaining the Beehive.

Anthropic heads for $1.3 trillion valuation in major stock market listing

Global · Major · Updated

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq on November 19, aiming to raise up to $64 billion at a valuation between $1.1 trillion and $1.3 trillion. The company reported revenues of $16.2 billion for the six months ending in June, though its pre-tax loss increased to $80.7 billion.

Why it matters

As the first fully AI-focused company to go public, Anthropic's listing serves as a test case for the future of the technology sector amid market volatility and concerns over the financial viability of massive AI investments.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

Global · United States · China · Singapore · Major · Updated

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials believe was recruited to spy for China. The company launched an independent investigation, and congressional leaders formally summoned Huang for a closed-door briefing on November 18 to address national security concerns.

Why it matters

The incident intersects with US-China geopolitical tensions and AI competition, as Nvidia's chips are critical to the US AI advantage and subject to strict export controls. The congressional inquiry highlights concerns that the relationship could have facilitated the transfer of sensitive technology or national security information to China.

Kāpiti Coast Airport asks Kāpiti Aero Club to relinquish its lease by end of month

NZ · Notable · Updated

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Kāpiti Coast Airport Holdings has asked the Kāpiti Aero Club to surrender its lease, which is valid until 2033, by 30 November and vacate the land by 26 February 2027. Sounds Air’s chief executive stated he was informed the airport will close on 30 November following a conditional sale agreement by owner NZ PropCo.

Economy · Environment · Politics

The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills

United Kingdom · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

UK energy bills are forecast to rise by over 25% in January, adding approximately £460 to typical household costs, as oil and gas prices soar following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The UK government approved the Jackdaw gas field while blocking a Chinese wind turbine factory, with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stating that affordability is her overriding objective. She noted that domestic oil and gas production will not lower bills because energy is sold on global markets, while the North Sea's output continues to decline.

Why it matters

The Climate Change Committee estimates that a future price shock would increase household bills by 59% on a high-carbon path, compared to 4% if Britain focused on renewables, highlighting the financial stakes of the energy policy choice.

Daily News

AI · Science · Technology

PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

Global · Major · Previously featured

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Physical Superintelligence (PSI) used Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve the 18-year-old Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a central open problem in quantum query complexity. The proof, autoformalized in Lean, indicates that quantum computers cannot solve certain difficult problems faster than classical ones via that specific avenue. PSI currently generates revenue by optimizing data centers but aims to convert theoretical physics breakthroughs into technologies, acknowledging that validating AI-generated results in the physical world remains a significant challenge.

Why it matters

The event highlights a shift in scientific discovery where AI models solve complex theoretical problems, prompting the academic community to develop new standards for verification and transparency as 'neolabs' emerge.

Conflict · Politics

Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes

Saudi Arabia · Yemen · Major · Previously featured

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Houthi forces launched missile and drone strikes on Riyadh, hitting the Aramco Tower in the central financial district, an airport, and oil storage facilities. The Saudi energy ministry reported only minor damage and no casualties, but BBC-verified footage showed extensive damage to multiple floors of the tower. Saudi air defenses intercepted several missiles, and the strikes followed a Houthi accusation that a Saudi-led coalition killed at least 33 people in Yemen.

Why it matters

The attacks mark a significant escalation in the conflict, with the Houthis targeting deep inside Saudi Arabia after an informal ceasefire collapsed in July amid the Iran war.

Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction

Russia · Major · Previously featured

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Researchers at Forschungszentrum Jülich identified that synchronized state-of-charge checks by internet-connected uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) cause global, minute-by-minute frequency drops on power grids. The study found that in Ireland, where data centers consume 18% of electricity, these drops quadrupled from 3 mHz in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021, with recent instances exceeding 20 mHz. The team recommends manufacturers randomize check schedules to prevent potential grid instability.

Why it matters

Unchecked frequency oscillations can damage hydropower equipment and, if combined with other grid loads, push systems toward blackout conditions. The issue requires global coordination as regulators can only address their specific grid segments.

Africa · Useful · Previously featured

Briefing produced 13 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa. A 2024 genomic analysis of 1,763 Africans found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa, supporting a population expansion from that region. Archaeological evidence, including pottery in the Congo rainforest dating to 2,300–2,000 years ago, suggests Bantu groups crossed the forest together before splitting into east- and south-moving groups 2,500 to 3,500 years ago.

Why it matters

The expansion reshaped sub-Saharan Africa's demography, introducing sedentary lifestyles and metalworking to hunter-gatherer regions. Today, approximately 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages, and many carry Bantu ancestry, making this one of history's largest human migrations.

A man in his 20s in the UK survived a knife piercing his right eye and brain, with the blade traversing the left frontal and temporal lobes without damaging the corpus callosum or major arteries. Doctors removed the blade via a conservative neurosurgical approach, and the patient recovered with preserved language and movement, though his right eye was removed.

Why it matters

The case illustrates that survival from low-velocity penetrating brain injuries depends on the precise trajectory relative to critical vascular and neural structures rather than the external severity of the wound.

Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub

Global · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 12 Nov 2026, 3:00 PM NZDT

Apiiro researchers found over 100,000 public GitHub repositories containing Claude Code's local settings files, with approximately 1,100 files from 63 organizations exposing secrets like API tokens and database passwords. The leak occurs because the global .gitignore setting is not reflected at the repository level, allowing the file to be accidentally committed. Anthropic's Boris Cherny stated the team is investigating prevention methods, while Apiiro noted that 215 of the discovered secrets were not flagged by popular scanners like gitleaks and TruffleHog.

Why it matters

The incident highlights a security vulnerability in AI coding tools where automated file handling can inadvertently expose sensitive credentials, posing risks to organizational data security even when standard local protections are in place.

Daily News

Technology · Science

Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery.

Global · Major · Catch up

Briefing produced 11 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Researchers at Forschungszentrum Jülich identified that synchronized state-of-charge checks by internet-connected uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) cause periodic 60-second frequency drops on global power grids. The study found that in Ireland, where data centers consume 18% of electricity, these drops quadrupled from 3 mHz in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021, with recent instances exceeding 20 mHz. The team recommends manufacturers randomize check schedules to prevent potential grid instability.

Why it matters

The phenomenon is preventable through software updates, but widespread adoption is hindered by low IoT firmware update rates, potentially requiring global regulatory coordination to avoid cumulative grid risks.

Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa.
Daily News

Science · Geography

The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.

Africa · Useful · Previously featured

Briefing produced 11 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa. A 2024 genomic analysis of 1,763 Africans found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa, supporting a population expansion from that region. Archaeological evidence, including pottery in the Congo rainforest dating to 2,300–2,000 years ago, suggests Bantu groups crossed the forest together before splitting into east- and south-moving groups 2,500 to 3,500 years ago.

Why it matters

The expansion reshaped sub-Saharan Africa's demography, introducing sedentary lifestyles and metalworking to hunter-gatherer regions. Today, approximately 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages, and many carry Bantu ancestry, making this one of history's largest human migrations.

Physicists used shot noise measurements to show that electron pairing in cuprate superconductors occurs at the pseudogap energy, supporting the theory that pre-formed pairs exist before superconductivity. The study, published in Science, found that pairing is associated with the pseudogap, ruling out the hypothesis that it arises solely from frozen electron patterns, though it does not exclude intertwined mechanisms.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that the bottleneck for higher-temperature superconductivity in cuprates is achieving phase coherence among pre-formed pairs, rather than forming the pairs themselves, which could guide future material design efforts.

The findings challenge the validity of current methods used to assess emotional resilience, a core component of cognitive behavioral therapy, and call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted.

A study in Nature proposes that slow mantle convection pushed the ancient continent of Laurentia up for hundreds of millions of years, creating a surface that glaciers then eroded to form the Great Unconformity. The researchers argue that this combination of gentle uplift and glacial scouring explains why the geological gap is prominent in North America but less distinct elsewhere, though they note that mantle dynamics were likely one of several contributing factors to the subsequent Cambrian explosion.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that deep Earth processes may have influenced the timing of the Cambrian explosion by washing eroded rock material into the oceans, potentially fertilizing them with calcium just before life began forming shells and skeletons.

The study, published in Science, found that pairing is associated with the pseudogap, ruling out the hypothesis that it arises solely from frozen electron patterns, though it does not exclude intertwined mechanisms.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that the bottleneck for higher-temperature superconductivity in cuprates is achieving phase coherence among pre-formed pairs, rather than forming the pairs themselves, which could guide future material design efforts.

Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity

Global · Notable · Previously featured

Briefing produced 09 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

A study in Nature proposes that slow mantle convection pushed the ancient continent of Laurentia up for hundreds of millions of years, creating a surface that glaciers then eroded to form the Great Unconformity. The researchers argue that this combination of gentle uplift and glacial scouring explains why the geological gap is prominent in North America but less distinct elsewhere, though they note that mantle dynamics were likely one of several contributing factors to the subsequent Cambrian explosion.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that deep Earth processes may have influenced the timing of the Cambrian explosion by washing eroded rock material into the oceans, potentially fertilizing them with calcium just before life began forming shells and skeletons.

Business · Science

Skin cancer patients pushed towards less effective treatment by insurance shortfalls

NZ · Useful · Catch up

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Southern Cross Health Insurance narrowed coverage criteria for Mohs surgery, a high-cure-rate skin cancer treatment, in December. Since April, patients have faced policy limits that force them to choose between Mohs and less effective standard excisions based on remaining funds. Dr AJ Seine of the NZ Dermatological Society warned that these financial constraints lead to poorer health decisions and increased complications, noting that standard incisions have a higher failure rate.

Why it matters

The shift from unlimited Mohs coverage to policy-limited funding creates a direct financial barrier to the internationally recognized gold standard treatment, potentially compromising patient outcomes for those with high-risk skin cancers.
